title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models

paper.title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout.
To connect the circuit’s Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with 303 303 shots per sample against a high-shot reference of 1.6 × 10 6 1.6\times 10^{6} , about 5300 × 5300\times fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.

sections.heading: I-A Motivation
sections.text: Quantum computing (QC) has attracted considerable attention due to its potential in computational advantages for certain classes of problems [ 25 , 29 ] . As a framework that combines parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) with modern machine-learning methods, quantum neural networks (QNNs) have consequently become an important research direction. Among their applications, quantum generative modeling aims to exploit quantum states, circuit dynamics, and measurement statistics to learn complex data distributions. The output of a quantum circuit is generally not available as an exact real-valued vector. Instead, the circuit must be measured repeatedly, and its output probabilities are estimated from a finite number of measurement shots. The resulting estimator inevitably contains finite-shot fluctuations. Taking more shots reduces these fluctuations but raises the cost of each QNN evaluation. Therefore, readout precision must be paid for in repeated circuit executions. Meanwhile, diffusion models (DMs) have achieved remarkable success in learning high-dimensional data distributions [ 33 , 13 , 36 , 30 ] . Unlike one-step direct generation methods, a denoising DM generates a sample through a sequence of reverse denoising steps rather than a single forward evaluation. Starting from random noise, the sampler repeatedly uses a denoiser to predict a clean sample from the current state and diffusion time. In this work, a QNN supplies this per-step denoising prediction, while the complete reverse loop generates a new sample. Stochastic samplers also inject noise during the reverse process, which provides the budget we seek to reuse. Stochastic diffusion sampling introduces a tension into this precision requirement. A conventional QNN-based sampler first spends measurements suppressing fluctuations in the denoising prediction, then explicitly injects fresh random noise into the reverse update. Some of the randomness removed at the readout is thus followed immediately by randomness added by the sampler. This raises the question motivating our work: can finite-shot measurement fluctuations supply part of the prescribed reverse-step noise, allowing us to measure less without sacrificing generation quality? A second issue is the mismatch between quantum measurement outputs and the data representation used by DMs. Standard DMs operate in Euclidean spaces, where coordinates may take positive or negative values and need not sum to one. In contrast, computational-basis measurements of a quantum circuit naturally produce probability vectors on the simplex. Although amplitude encoding can represent signed information at the state-vector level, direct measurements still return probabilities. Angular encoding is straightforward to implement using parameterized rotations, but generally requires a number of qubits that grows linearly with the input dimension. Probability encoding is therefore attractive for direct quantum readout, provided that Euclidean data and the denoising target can be connected to it. To reconcile these representations, we formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane and connect this space to the probability simplex through an affine transformation. Both the noisy input and the clean denoising target can then be represented as probability vectors, without reconstructing signed amplitudes from measurement outcomes. A trainable linear readout maps the circuit probabilities back into the data space. Finite-shot readout is characterized by multinomial sampling, so its covariance can be propagated explicitly through this map and compared with the noise prescribed by the reverse step. The central idea of this work is to align this finite-shot measurement noise with the stochasticity of the reverse diffusion process. When the QNN output is estimated using a limited number of shots, the estimator contains a random perturbation whose covariance is determined by the predicted probability distribution and the measurement budget. By accounting for this covariance in the reverse update, the measurement-induced perturbation can contribute to the total stochasticity required by the sampler, and thereby replace part of the externally injected diffusion noise. Under-sampling is thus no longer viewed merely as an approximation to exact quantum readout, but as a mechanism for redistributing the required randomness between quantum measurement and classical noise injection. This perspective naturally leads to a shot-adaptive quantum diffusion sampler. In reverse steps with a relatively large stochastic noise budget, fewer measurements may be used because a larger portion of the finite-shot uncertainty can be absorbed into the sampling dynamics. In steps that require a more accurate denoising estimate, additional shots can be assigned to reduce measurement variance. The number of shots should therefore be scheduled according to the step-dependent noise level and the covariance structure of the quantum measurement estimator, rather than fixed conservatively throughout the entire sampling trajectory.

sections.heading: I-B Related Works
sections.text: This work lies at the intersection of diffusion-based generative modeling and QC. In the following, we review the related works from both quantum computing and diffusion aspects, and introduce other existing combinations. QC uses qubits as its basic carriers of information and processes that information in an exponentially large state space through superposition and entanglement. One family of models that is convenient to optimize is the PQC, built from stacked layers of tunable quantum gates and trained by iterating over its parameters much as a neural network is [ 4 , 8 , 28 ] . Unlike a classical network, the output of a quantum circuit cannot be read out directly. Instead the circuit is measured repeatedly in the computational basis, and the probability of each basis state is estimated from a finite number of measurement outcomes, following the Born rule [ 25 ] . The readout of a quantum circuit therefore carries an intrinsic sampling noise from this finite measurement, whose magnitude decreases as the number of measurements grows. This sampling noise is the common starting point of later work on measurement cost, and it is the object that we revisit in this paper. Building on QC, quantum machine learning studies how PQCs can carry out learning tasks [ 5 , 31 , 12 , 23 ] . A central step is how classical data is loaded into a quantum state, for which common encodings include amplitude encoding, angle encoding, and data re-uploading [ 27 , 19 ] . The choice of encoding determines not only the form in which data enters the circuit but also the class of functions the circuit can express and how easily it can be trained [ 32 , 22 , 1 ] . A recurring practical obstacle in this area is the readout issue noted above. The circuit output is available only through repeated measurements, the readout fluctuates when the number of measurements is small, and the usual remedy is to take more measurements, which directly raises the computational cost. Our work departs from this common practice. Rather than treating the fluctuation as an error to be suppressed, we attend to its structure and put it to use. Parallel to this quantum-computing thread are DMs, including denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM) and score-based generative models [ 13 , 35 , 36 , 24 ] . Stochastic samplers inject Gaussian noise during reverse sampling. The denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) also permits deterministic generation from different random initial states [ 34 ] . Our method uses the noise prescribed by a stochastic sampler as a budget for finite-shot measurement error. Using a PQC as the denoising generator of a DM is a more recent line at this intersection. Quantum generative models have been explored fairly widely, with quantum circuit Born machines and quantum generative adversarial networks as basic architectures [ 3 , 20 , 21 , 10 , 40 ] , and on this basis quantum and hybrid DMs have appeared more recently [ 39 , 26 , 16 , 7 , 18 ] . Existing quantum diffusion studies mostly realize the forward and reverse processes with a parameterized circuit and assume that high-precision circuit outputs are available, so that the overall measurement cost rises together with the required readout accuracy. Broadly, prior work tends to regard the finite-shot measurement error as an approximation error and suppresses it by taking more measurements. This is the point that our work seeks to handle differently. Reducing the measurement and sampling cost of QC is therefore a line of research in its own right. Existing schemes include allocating measurements across different observables in variational algorithms, and constructing classical estimates of a quantum state from a small number of measurements [ 38 , 37 , 9 , 17 , 2 , 11 , 14 ] . What these methods share is the goal of keeping the estimation error small with limited measures. Meanwhile, our starting point is different from both threads above. Generally speaking, the quantum diffusion works assume the requirement of an accurate readout and pay for it. The measurement-frugal works minimize the estimation error under a shot budget. Both therefore treat the error as something to be made small. Instead of minimizing the readout error, we only seek to limit it such that the generation procedure can work normally, making a covariance matching problem instead of minimizing. Where such condition holds, the sampler reduces the injected-noise covariance by the covariance already contributed by measurement. The shot count is then an output of the condition rather than a hyperparameter to be tuned, and it is what our adaptive schedule implements.

sections.heading: I-C Contributions
sections.text: The contribution of this work mainly lies on a QC mechanism for diffusion model applications. We turn the finite-shot noise of a quantum readout from a liability into a resource the sampler can spend, and we give the condition that says how far it can be spent. The specific contributions are as follows. • We identify the injected-noise covariance of a stochastic diffusion sampler as a budget for finite-shot readout noise, allowing quantum measurement fluctuations to replace part of the externally generated noise. • We derive a positive-semidefinite (PSD) condition for matching the total conditional noise covariance to that of the shot-noise-free reverse step, and solve it for a state-dependent shot budget. With the true covariance and conditionally independent residual noise, this gives exact covariance matching for the linear update, which additionally relies on the Gaussian approximation to the readout error. • We supply the encoding and the trainable readout that the mechanism needs, placing the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex so that the Born-measurement output is compatible with the denoising task. • We validate the method on a Gaussian mixture and on MNIST in a learned latent space, achieving comparable quality on the reported metrics with far fewer measurements.

sections.heading: II-B Basics on Quantum Computing
sections.text: In QC, we typically use amplitude encoding or angular encoding, which is realized by rotation gates, to encode the raw input into quantum states. Specifically, if we have an N N -dimensional input 𝒙 = ( x 1 , ⋯ , x N ) ⊤ ∈ ℛ N \bm{x}=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{N})^{\top}\in\mathcal{R}^{N} , the amplitude encoding becomes | x ⟩ = 1 ‖ 𝒙 ‖ 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 N x i ​ | i ⟩ , \ket{x}=\frac{1}{\|\bm{x}\|_{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}\ket{i}, (6) where | i ⟩ \ket{i} is represented by ⌈ log 2 ⁡ N ⌉ \lceil\log_{2}N\rceil qubits corresponding to the binary representation of i i . Meanwhile, the angular encoding is defined as | x ⟩ = ⨂ i = 1 N ( cos ⁡ ( x i / 2 ) ​ | 0 ⟩ + sin ⁡ ( x i / 2 ) ​ | 1 ⟩ ) , \ket{x}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{N}\left(\cos(x_{i}/2)\ket{0}+\sin(x_{i}/2)\ket{1}\right), (7) where ⨂ \bigotimes represents the concatenation of quantum states. Thus, angular encoding requires N N qubits. We also have another simple encoding scheme called probability encoding, which is similar to the amplitude encoding that | p ⟩ = ∑ i = 1 N p i ​ | i ⟩ , \ket{p}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sqrt{p_{i}}\ket{i}, (8) which requires that the input 𝒑 \bm{p} is in the probabilistic space 𝒫 N − 1 ≜ { 𝒙 | 𝒙 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] N , ∥ 𝒙 ∥ 1 = 1 } \mathcal{P}^{N-1}\triangleq\{\bm{x}|\bm{x}\in[0,1]^{N},\|\bm{x}\|_{1}=1\} .

sections.heading: II-C Quantum Neural Networks
sections.text: A QNN is a quantum circuit U ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) U(\bm{\theta}) whose gate operations depend on a set of trainable parameters 𝜽 \bm{\theta} . Its operation can be described in three steps, by analogy with a classical neural network. The input is first encoded into a quantum state | ψ in ⟩ \ket{\psi_{\mathrm{in}}} . The parameterized circuit then acts on it to give the output state | ψ out ⟩ = U ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) ​ | ψ in ⟩ \ket{\psi_{\mathrm{out}}}=U(\bm{\theta})\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{in}}} , and a measurement in the computational basis reads out the Born probabilities p i = | ⟨ i | ψ out ⟩ | 2 p_{i}=|\braket{i|\psi_{\mathrm{out}}}|^{2} of the basis states. As in a classical network, the parameters 𝜽 \bm{\theta} are trained by gradient descent to minimize a task loss ℒ ⁡ ( 𝜽 ) \mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}) , which for the diffusion denoiser of this paper is specified in Section III-D . A common circuit structure stacks L L layers of identical form. As shown in Fig. 1 , each layer consists of two parts. The first is a set of single-qubit parameterized rotations R Y ( θ ) = e − i θ Y / 2 R_{Y}(\theta)=e^{-i\theta Y/2} and R Z ( θ ) = e − i θ Z / 2 R_{Z}(\theta)=e^{-i\theta Z/2} , with Y Y and Z Z the Pauli matrices, applied to every qubit. The second is a fixed entangling block, for instance a ring of CNOT gates that connects the qubits end to end, which correlates the qubits. Writing 𝑽 l ​ ( 𝜽 l ) \bm{V}_{l}(\bm{\theta}_{l}) for the combined rotation-and-entangling operation of layer l l , the circuit is their composition U ( 𝜽 ) = 𝑽 L ( 𝜽 L ) ⋯ 𝑽 1 ( 𝜽 1 ) U(\bm{\theta})=\bm{V}_{L}(\bm{\theta}_{L})\cdots\bm{V}_{1}(\bm{\theta}_{1}) . To give a circuit of modest depth enough expressive power, the input features can be re-injected into the rotation angles of every layer, a technique known as data re-uploading [ 27 , 32 ] . By feeding the same input into different layers repeatedly, a shallow circuit can represent more complex functions. In this work, we consider the implementation of DM with a QNN, whose structure is illustrated in Fig. 1 . The QNN takes the encoded noisy sample and the current diffusion step as input. The input is first loaded into | q ⁡ ( τ ) ⟩ \ket{q(\tau)} with time embedding through quantum encoding, whose details are discussed in the following section. After L L layers of rotations and CNOT rings as in Fig. 1 , the result is measured in the computational basis to give the estimate 𝒑 ~ \tilde{\bm{p}} of the probability. A readout layer then decodes 𝒑 ~ \tilde{\bm{p}} into a prediction of the clean signal. It is a classical linear layer applied to the measurement outcomes, which is not a part of the quantum circuit.

sections.heading: III Diffusion Model on Probabilistic Space
sections.text: Figure 2 compares two sampling pipelines for quantum diffusion models using the same QNN denoiser and classical readout. At each reverse step, the QNN predicts the clean sample from the current noisy state and diffusion time. Conventional sampling uses many shots to suppress measurement noise, then adds the full prescribed diffusion noise. Our sampler uses fewer shots and reduces the added noise to account for the measurement fluctuations. Both start from random noise: denoising is the prediction at each step, and generation is the complete reverse loop. Fig. 2: QNN diffusion sampling with (a) conventional high-shot readout and (b) adaptive under-sampling that reuses measurement noise.

sections.heading: III-A Hybrid Encoding for Quantum Diffusion Models
sections.text: For a DM, the encoding is not a free design choice, and we begin by making the constraint that fixes it explicit. A DM applies its denoiser iteratively. The output of one reverse step is the input of the next, so the encoding and the readout must live in the same space. On the quantum side the readout is fixed by physics, since measuring in the computational basis returns Born probabilities and the output of the circuit therefore always lies in the simplex 𝒫 N − 1 \mathcal{P}^{N-1} . The input must consequently be placed on the simplex as well, and probability encoding, which loads p i \sqrt{p_{i}} into the amplitude of | i ⟩ \ket{i} , is the encoding that the problem selects. The other two encodings of Section II-B play different roles here. Angle encoding uses one qubit per data dimension, and we adopt it in Section IV-C , where a low data dimension makes it affordable. Amplitude encoding is more expressive per qubit, but its output is a probability vector while its input is a signed amplitude vector, so the two do not live in the same space and the denoiser cannot be iterated without an extra and costly reconstruction step. Probability encoding leaves one resource untouched. It fixes only the moduli of the amplitudes and says nothing about their phases, so the azimuthal degrees of freedom of the state are unused. A DM, in turn, must supply its denoiser with one quantity beyond the noisy sample, namely the current diffusion step, which is conventionally injected through a time embedding. The information the denoiser has to carry is thus exactly the information the encoding has room for. We therefore write the diffusion step into the phases, which gives the following hybrid encoding of probability and time, | p ⁡ ( t ) ⟩ ≜ ∑ i = 1 N p i ​ e j ​ f i ​ ( t ) ​ | i ⟩ , \ket{p(t)}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sqrt{p_{i}}e^{jf_{i}(t)}\ket{i}, (9) where 𝒑 ∈ 𝒫 N − 1 \bm{p}\in\mathcal{P}^{N-1} is the input and 𝒇 ⁡ ( t ) \bm{f}(t) is the time embedding. The probability encoding requires the entries of 𝒑 \bm{p} to sum to one, so an n q n_{q} -qubit state, which carries N = 2 n q N=2^{n_{q}} probabilities, has only N − 1 = 2 n q − 1 N-1=2^{n_{q}}-1 independent degrees of freedom. The generative task is therefore represented on an ( N − 1 ) (N-1) -dimensional space. We write the diffusion step into the phases by letting the phase of basis state i i advance linearly in the normalized step τ ≜ t / ( T − 1 ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \tau\triangleq t/(T-1)\in[0,1] , f i ( τ ) ≜ c w i τ , w i ≜ a i + b i 2 , i = 1 , … , N , f_{i}(\tau)\triangleq c\,w_{i}\,\tau,\qquad w_{i}\triangleq a\,i+b\,i^{2},\qquad i=1,\dots,N, (10) with a , b > 0 a,b>0 shaping the rates across the basis and c > 0 c>0 setting their overall scale. We fix that scale so the largest phase excursion ϕ max \phi_{\max} stays within one revolution, c = ϕ max a ​ N + b ​ N 2 , ϕ max ∈ ( 0 , 2 ​ π ] , c=\frac{\phi_{\max}}{aN+bN^{2}},\qquad\phi_{\max}\in(0,2\pi], (11) so that the embedding is controlled by the single scalar ϕ max \phi_{\max} , while a a and b b only redistribute the phase budget across the basis. Amplitude encoding and probability encoding place the state at different polar angles, using the probability values and their square roots as amplitudes respectively, and a natural property of the latter is that the Born probabilities obtained from measurement equal the input distribution. The hybrid encoding builds on probability encoding and writes the diffusion step into the azimuthal phase. Switching off the time embedding removes that phase, so the fourth and fifth schemes in Fig. 3 coincide with the first and the second. sections.text: The absorption mechanism derived above is a statement about the reverse process, not about the probability encoding, and it is instructive to instantiate it for a different encoding. We do so for the angle encoding of Section III-A , in which every coordinate is carried by its own qubit. The resulting scheme is of independent interest because its readout contains no trainable parameters at all, so that whatever denoising takes place must take place inside the circuit. sections.heading: V Mechanism Illustration and Validation on a Gaussian Mixture
sections.text: We begin with a Gaussian mixture. The data lives on the zero-sum hyperplane, so the task is a degenerate seven-dimensional distribution embedded in ℝ 8 \mathbb{R}^{8} . A mixture of this kind is easy to visualize and its ground truth is known exactly, which is what we need in order to check that the under-sampled quantum sampler still recovers several modes instead of collapsing onto one. It also lets us take the predictions of Section IV one at a time, namely the shape of the shot budget ( 32 ), the two bounds that clamp it, the cost of determinism of Corollary 2 , what the trainable readout contributes, and the per-dimension variant of Section IV-C .

The sampler starts from an isotropic cloud on the hyperplane and the three modes pull apart only over the last few steps, once the injected noise σ t \sigma_{t} has become small and the denoiser has to be accurate. sections.heading: V-C The Adaptive Shot Budget
sections.text: The budget ( 32 ) is recomputed at every reverse step from the current state, and Fig. 7 shows the profile it produces for reverse processes of ten, twenty, and fifty steps. All three trace the same shape. The demand sits on the lower bound M min M_{\mathrm{min}} over the early part of the trajectory, where the sampler measures as little as the clamp allows, and then climbs steeply toward the end, with more than half of the total spent on the last two steps alone. Section IV-B predicts this. The injected noise σ t \sigma_{t} is large early on and can absorb a very coarse readout, and it shrinks as the trajectory proceeds, where the readout has to become accurate. The three schedules also spend a similar total, so the profile is set by the noise schedule rather than by the number of reverse steps. The same total budget can buy very different quality depending on how it is spread. Fig. 8 makes that comparison against a uniform allocation over the same twenty steps. At a matched budget of a few hundred shots per sample the adaptive schedule is well ahead, and the uniform one needs about four times as many measurements before it catches up on the resolved fraction. Spreading the measurements evenly wastes them on steps that do not need them and starves the steps that do. The gap is widest in the low-budget regime, which is the regime that matters for quantum sampling. Fig. 7: Shots per reverse step under the adaptive budget ( 32 ). Fig. 8: Adaptive versus uniform shot allocation.

sections.heading: V-D The Bounds on the Budget
sections.text: The budget ( 32 ) has only two free parameters and they come from different places. The lower bound M min M_{\mathrm{min}} is a modelling safeguard. Theorem 1 is a central-limit statement, and the usual rule of thumb for the multinomial CLT asks for M ​ p i ≳ 5 Mp_{i}\gtrsim 5 , which at p i ≈ 1 / N p_{i}\approx 1/N would demand M ≳ 5 ​ N = 40 M\gtrsim 5N=40 . The upper bound M max M_{\mathrm{max}} is a resource limit set by what measurement costs. Fig. 9 sweeps them one at a time, the lower bound on the left and the upper bound on the right. Raising the lower shot bound from 2 to 64 leaves the resolved fraction essentially unchanged and MMD 2 \mathrm{MMD}^{2} unchanged within its standard deviation, while increasing cost by about a factor of four and a half. The two-shot steps occur mainly early in the trajectory, where the noise budget is large. We therefore select M min = 2 M_{\mathrm{min}}=2 empirically, despite operating outside the Gaussian-approximation regime. The upper bound behaves in the opposite way. It truncates ( 32 ) where the budget is largest, at the final steps, so a cap below the peak demand leaves the PSD condition ( 31 ) unsatisfied. The residual covariance then acquires negative eigenvalues, which are clipped to zero. For the true-covariance model, this removes external noise in the affected directions, but cannot remove measurement noise that already exceeds the target. The resulting failure is a mismatch in total noise covariance, not a shortage of injected randomness. The effect is severe. As M max M_{\mathrm{max}} rises from below the peak demand, the resolved fraction climbs steeply while the saturated fraction falls, and once the cap clears the peak the saturated fraction reaches zero and the resolved fraction settles at the value of the unclamped schedule. Quality tracks the saturated fraction rather than the total budget, which is the signature of a broken covariance contract and not of a shortage of measurements. We use M min = 2 M_{\mathrm{min}}=2 and M max = 2 × 10 5 M_{\mathrm{max}}=2\times 10^{5} : the lower bound saves measurements in early steps, while the upper bound remains above peak demand and never becomes active. sections.heading: V-E Injected Noise and the Cost of Determinism
sections.text: The parameter η \eta picks a member of the DDIM family, from the deterministic sampler at η = 0 \eta=0 to the stochastic DDPM sampler at η = 1 \eta=1 , and the framework of Section IV covers all of them. Generation quality bears this out. Across the sweep of Fig. 10 the resolved fraction is essentially unchanged, so any member of the family may be used, DDIM and DDPM alike. The measurement cost is another matter, and Corollary 2 says how it should behave. A sampler made more deterministic has to be measured more, at a rate of 1 / η 2 1/\eta^{2} . The sweep follows that law closely wherever the budget sits well above its lower bound, where halving η \eta costs about a factor of 3.8 3.8 , close to the predicted 4 4 . As η \eta grows the budget falls onto M min M_{\mathrm{min}} over the early steps, the clamp takes over, and the growth flattens toward the stochastic end. The deterministic limit is the extreme case. At zero stochasticity, the prescribed update has no injected-noise budget for compensation. We therefore use the capped high-shot setting in this comparison; its cost is four orders of magnitude above that of the stochastic sampler. Any remaining finite-shot error is an uncompensated approximation to the deterministic update. Across this sweep, generation quality remains approximately flat while measurement cost falls toward the stochastic end. We therefore use η = 1 \eta=1 , the least expensive setting in the comparison. sections.heading: V-F The Role of the Readout
sections.text: Section IV-A makes a specific claim about the linear readout, that it reshapes the covariance of the finite-shot noise into 𝚵 ​ 𝐖 ⊤ ​ 𝚺 ​ 𝐖 ​ 𝚵 \mathbf{\Xi}\mathbf{W}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{\Xi} rather than simply rescaling it, and so changes how many shots the sampler needs. The upper block of Table I tests this inside the logarithmic encoding, with the frozen affine decoding of Corollary 1 on one side and our default diagonal readout, which carries N N parameters, on the other. The frozen readout loses on both axes. Its resolved fraction is markedly lower and it demands roughly thirty times as many shots. Training the readout therefore improves the fit and cuts the measurement cost at the same time, which is the behaviour ( 32 ) would lead one to expect. A readout that steers the shaped covariance into directions the diffusion noise can absorb lowers its largest eigenvalue, and the budget follows. It does so without growing large. The analytic scale of the readout is A ​ N AN , while the learned diagonal readout settles at a spectral norm some seven times smaller, because the circuit learns to output probabilities further from uniform, so a smaller gain already covers the data range. This comparison does not by itself isolate how much denoising is supplied by the trainable readout. The fixed affine baseline uses 𝐖 = A ​ N ​ 𝐈 8 = 24 ​ 𝐈 8 \mathbf{W}=AN\mathbf{I}_{8}=24\mathbf{I}_{8} and 𝒃 = − A ​ 𝟏 \bm{b}=-A\bm{1} , with A = 3 A=3 and N = 8 N=8 , where 𝐈 8 \mathbf{I}_{8} is the eight-dimensional identity matrix. The factor A ​ N AN reverses the scaling of ( 16 ) such that probability deviations must be converted back to data units. In the unclipped regime, the baseline requires the circuit to produce the prescribed probability target accurately, which is demanding for twelve layers on three qubits. The per-dimension encoding of Section IV-C settles it. Its readout ( 36 ) is the exact inverse of its own encoding rather than something imposed from outside, so it carries no trainable parameters and nothing has to be matched, and whatever denoising happens has to happen inside the circuit. We run it on the same mixture with n q = N = 8 n_{q}=N=8 qubits, the same diffusion schedule, and the per-dimension budget ( 39 ). The lower block of Table I and the last panel of Fig. 11 report what comes out. The adaptive sampler again matches the shot-noise-free readout, here at about 1600 × 1600\times fewer measurements. The comparison with the frozen row is the point. With no trainable readout parameters at all the per-dimension encoding reaches the same quality, whereas the same absence of parameters noticeably lowers the resolved fraction of the logarithmic encoding. The structural learning is thus done by the quantum circuit, and the trainable readout of the logarithmic encoding improves the fit and the measurement cost without being the agent of the denoising. The absorption mechanism and the adaptive schedule carry over unchanged to an encoding whose finite-shot covariance is diagonal rather than multinomial, as Section IV-C predicts. The price is the qubit count, which grows from log 2 ⁡ N \log_{2}N to N N , and that is what keeps the per-dimension encoding to low-dimensional data until a code reduces the dimension, as in Section VI-C . sections.heading: V-G Ablation on the Encoding and the Time Embedding
sections.text: We close by isolating the encoding of Section III-A . Table II crosses the three encodings with the presence or absence of the time embedding, five runs each, everything else held fixed. Switching the time embedding off removes the azimuthal phase, at which point the hybrid encoding coincides with probability encoding by construction, and the two rows agree. The time embedding is not optional. Removing it raises the MMD 2 \mathrm{MMD}^{2} by a factor of 3 ∼ 4 3\sim 4 for every encoding and drops the resolved fraction below 0.89 0.89 . A denoiser that cannot tell which diffusion step it is on cannot invert the forward process, and that is the dominant effect in the table. With the time embedding present, the hybrid encoding is the best on both metrics, ahead of probability encoding and amplitude encoding. The margin over probability encoding is what writing the diffusion step into the free phases is worth, and it costs no qubits. sections.heading: VI Image Generation Examples
sections.text: We next apply the method to MNIST in a learned latent space. To keep the quantum circuit small, we compress each 28 × 28 = 784 28\times 28=784 -pixel image into a low-dimensional latent. A fixed variational autoencoder (VAE) supplies this representation and the image decoder. The QNN predicts the clean latent at each reverse step; the full loop starts from random latent noise and generates a new sample, which the VAE decodes into an image. We test the trainable-diagonal and fixed per-dimension readouts, then increase the latent dimension.

sections.heading: VI-A VAE-Based Compression
sections.text: We compress each image into a low-dimensional latent with a variational autoencoder (VAE) [ 15 ] . It produces the K = 7 K=7 latent coordinates that we lift onto the eight-dimensional zero-sum hyperplane, then rescale and clip as in Section III-B . The round trip through the VAE keeps the digits intact, and Fig. 13 shows this before the sampler is run at all. The real row and the VAE row carry the same legible digits, and a classifier that scores 97.1 % 97.1\% on the originals still reaches 94.4 % 94.4\% on the reconstructions. Working in this latent therefore ties the quantum resource to the latent dimension rather than to the image resolution, and we use it for the remainder of this section. Fig. 13: MNIST examples: real images and VAE reconstructions (top two rows), followed by QNN-generated samples from latent diffusion, decoded by the VAE.

sections.heading: VI-B Latent-Domain Quantum DDPM
sections.text: The QNN retains the same role as in the Gaussian-mixture experiment: it predicts the clean state from the current noisy iterate and the diffusion time. Here, the data coordinates come from the fixed VAE encoder. Its seven latent coordinates are lifted onto the eight-dimensional zero-sum hyperplane and processed by the same hybrid probability-and-time-phase encoding, a three-qubit circuit with 20 re-uploading layers, and a trainable diagonal readout. We train the denoiser to predict the clean latent state over 1,000 diffusion steps and use the same shot-adaptive reverse sampler for generation. Each generated trajectory begins with random noise. The final state is mapped back to the seven VAE coordinates and decoded into a 28-by-28 image, without post-processing. The three-qubit row of Fig. 13 shows generated samples covering all ten digit classes, with 49.1 % 49.1\% receiving classifier confidence above 0.9. The classifier is used only for evaluation. The efficiency result of Section IV carries over to real images unchanged. The adaptive schedule reaches MMD 2 = 0.0312 \mathrm{MMD}^{2}=0.0312 in image space with 430 430 shots per generated sample, about 3700 × 3700\times fewer measurements than the shot-noise-free readout at matched quality. It also survives a larger latent. The four-qubit row of Fig. 13 grows the latent to K = 15 K=15 , and the digits stay legible at MMD 2 = 0.0259 \mathrm{MMD}^{2}=0.0259 with a saving of about 2400 × 2400\times , so the mechanism is not tied to a single latent dimension.

sections.heading: VI-C Per-Dimension Encoding in the Latent Domain
sections.text: The per-dimension encoding of Section IV-C offers an alternative to the logarithmic probability encoding. Coordinate i i is carried by qubit i i and read back through the fixed map ( 36 ), so the readout holds no trainable parameters and whatever denoising happens has to happen inside the circuit. Its cost is a qubit count linear in the data dimension, which rules it out in pixel space, since a 784 784 -pixel image would call for 784 784 qubits. That is why the encoding has so far been confined to low-dimensional synthetic data. The latent formulation removes the obstacle. With only 8 8 dimensions to carry, we can run both encodings on the same latent, under the same diffusion schedule and the same under-sampling rule. The eight-qubit row of Fig. 13 shows the result. With 8 8 qubits and a fixed readout, the model reaches MMD 2 = 0.0143 \mathrm{MMD}^{2}=0.0143 in image space using 993 993 shots per sample, about 1600 × 1600\times fewer than the shot-noise-free readout, and 55.1 % 55.1\% of its samples are classified confidently. It is the best of the three configurations. The readout carries no free parameters, so the denoising is the work of the quantum circuit alone. That this configuration matches the trainable-readout model, and here slightly exceeds it, reproduces on images what Section V-F found on the mixture.

sections.heading: VII Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that finite-shot quantum measurement noise can supply part of the randomness a stochastic diffusion sampler would otherwise inject. Three elements make this possible. A bounded zero-sum representation mapped to the probability simplex connects the circuit’s Born probabilities to the denoising task. A trainable linear readout determines how measurement fluctuations enter the reverse update. A PSD condition then identifies how much of the prescribed noise covariance these fluctuations can supply, with classical noise filling the remainder. Under the stated assumptions, this compensation matches the conditional moments of the linear update; distribution matching additionally relies on a Gaussian approximation. Solving the condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget that increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the adaptive schedule achieves comparable generation quality with 303 303 shots per sample against 1.6 × 10 6 1.6\times 10^{6} for the high-shot reference. A uniform allocation needs about four times as many shots to match it, and the same mechanism supports MNIST generation in a learned latent space. Several directions remain open. The framework assumes a linear readout, and whether a nonlinear one admits a comparable covariance contract is not obvious. The budget bounds are set by hand. Further analysis is needed to quantify the effects of non-Gaussian finite-shot errors, estimated residual covariances, boundary projections, and denoiser approximation on the generated distribution. Finally, the scheme has so far been validated in simulation, where finite-shot noise is the only source of error. On hardware it coexists with gate and decoherence errors, whose covariance is not multinomial, and whether the reverse process can absorb those as well is the natural next question.

Abstract In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. To connect the circuit’s Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with 303 303 shots per sample against a high-shot reference of 1.6 × 10 6 1.6\times 10^{6} , about 5300 × 5300\times fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space. Index Terms: Quantum diffusion models, quantum machine learning, parameterized quantum circuits, finite-shot measurement noise, adaptive measurement allocation. I Introduction I-A Motivation Quantum computing (QC) has attracted considerable attention due to its potential in computational advantages for certain classes of problems [ 25 , 29 ] . As a framework that combines parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) with modern machine-learning methods, quantum neural networks (QNNs) have consequently become an important research direction. Among their applications, quantum generative modeling aims to exploit quantum states, circuit dynamics, and measurement statistics to learn complex data distributions. The output of a quantum circuit is generally not available as an exact real-valued vector. Instead, the circuit must be measured repeatedly, and its output probabilities are estimated from a finite number of measurement shots. The resulting estimator inevitably contains finite-shot fluctuations. Taking more shots reduces these fluctuations but raises the cost of each QNN evaluation. Therefore, readout precision must be paid for in repeated circuit executions. Meanwhile, diffusion models (DMs) have achieved remarkable success in learning high-dimensional data distributions [ 33 , 13 , 36 , 30 ] . Unlike one-step direct generation methods, a denoising DM generates a sample through a sequence of reverse denoising steps rather than a single forward evaluation. Starting from random noise, the sampler repeatedly uses a denoiser to predict a clean sample from the current state and diffusion time. In this work, a QNN supplies this per-step denoising prediction, while the complete reverse loop generates a new sample. Stochastic samplers also inject noise during the reverse process, which provides the budget we seek to reuse. Stochastic diffusion sampling introduces a tension into this precision requirement. A conventional QNN-based sampler first spends measurements suppressing fluctuations in the denoising prediction, then explicitly injects fresh random noise into the reverse update. Some of the randomness removed at the readout is thus followed immediately by randomness added by the sampler. This raises the question motivating our work: can finite-shot measurement fluctuations supply part of the prescribed reverse-step noise, allowing us to measure less without sacrificing generation quality? A second issue is the mismatch between quantum measurement outputs and the data representation used by DMs. Standard DMs operate in Euclidean spaces, where coordinates may take positive or negative values and need not sum to one. In contrast, computational-basis measurements of a quantum circuit naturally produce probability vectors on the simplex. Although amplitude encoding can represent signed information at the state-vector level, direct measurements still return probabilities. Angular encoding is straightforward to implement using parameterized rotations, but generally requires a number of qubits that grows linearly with the input dimension. Probability encoding is therefore attractive for direct quantum readout, provided that Euclidean data and the denoising target can be connected to it. To reconcile these representations, we formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane and connect this space to the probability simplex through an affine transformation. Both the noisy input and the clean denoising target can then be represented as probability vectors, without reconstructing signed amplitudes from measurement outcomes. A trainable linear readout maps the circuit probabilities back into the data space. Finite-shot readout is characterized by multinomial sampling, so its covariance can be propagated explicitly through this map and compared with the noise prescribed by the reverse step. The central idea of this work is to align this finite-shot measurement noise with the stochasticity of the reverse diffusion process. When the QNN output is estimated using a limited number of shots, the estimator contains a random perturbation whose covariance is determined by the predicted probability distribution and the measurement budget. By accounting for this covariance in the reverse update, the measurement-induced perturbation can contribute to the total stochasticity required by the sampler, and thereby replace part of the externally injected diffusion noise. Under-sampling is thus no longer viewed merely as an approximation to exact quantum readout, but as a mechanism for redistributing the required randomness between quantum measurement and classical noise injection. This perspective naturally leads to a shot-adaptive quantum diffusion sampler. In reverse steps with a relatively large stochastic noise budget, fewer measurements may be used because a larger portion of the finite-shot uncertainty can be absorbed into the sampling dynamics. In steps that require a more accurate denoising estimate, additional shots can be assigned to reduce measurement variance. The number of shots should therefore be scheduled according to the step-dependent noise level and the covariance structure of the quantum measurement estimator, rather than fixed conservatively throughout the entire sampling trajectory. I-B Related Works This work lies at the intersection of diffusion-based generative modeling and QC. In the following, we review the related works from both quantum computing and diffusion aspects, and introduce other existing combinations. QC uses qubits as its basic carriers of information and processes that information in an exponentially large state space through superposition and entanglement. One family of models that is convenient to optimize is the PQC, built from stacked layers of tunable quantum gates and trained by iterating over its parameters much as a neural network is [ 4 , 8 , 28 ] . Unlike a classical network, the output of a quantum circuit cannot be read out directly. Instead the circuit is measured repeatedly in the computational basis, and the probability of each basis state is estimated from a finite number of measurement outcomes, following the Born rule [ 25 ] . The readout of a quantum circuit therefore carries an intrinsic sampling noise from this finite measurement, whose magnitude decreases as the number of measurements grows. This sampling noise is the common starting point of later work on measurement cost, and it is the object that we revisit in this paper. Building on QC, quantum machine learning studies how PQCs can carry out learning tasks [ 5 , 31 , 12 , 23 ] . A central step is how classical data is loaded into a quantum state, for which common encodings include amplitude encoding, angle encoding, and data re-uploading [ 27 , 19 ] . The choice of encoding determines not only the form in which data enters the circuit but also the class of functions the circuit can express and how easily it can be trained [ 32 , 22 , 1 ] . A recurring practical obstacle in this area is the readout issue noted above. The circuit output is available only through repeated measurements, the readout fluctuates when the number of measurements is small, and the usual remedy is to take more measurements, which directly raises the computational cost. Our work departs from this common practice. Rather than treating the fluctuation as an error to be suppressed, we attend to its structure and put it to use. Parallel to this quantum-computing thread are DMs, including denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM) and score-based generative models [ 13 , 35 , 36 , 24 ] . Stochastic samplers inject Gaussian noise during reverse sampling. The denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) also permits deterministic generation from different random initial states [ 34 ] . Our method uses the noise prescribed by a stochastic sampler as a budget for finite-shot measurement error. Using a PQC as the denoising generator of a DM is a more recent line at this intersection. Quantum generative models have been explored fairly widely, with quantum circuit Born machines and quantum generative adversarial networks as basic architectures [ 3 , 20 , 21 , 10 , 40 ] , and on this basis quantum and hybrid DMs have appeared more recently [ 39 , 26 , 16 , 7 , 18 ] . Existing quantum diffusion studies mostly realize the forward and reverse processes with a parameterized circuit and assume that high-precision circuit outputs are available, so that the overall measurement cost rises together with the required readout accuracy. Broadly, prior work tends to regard the finite-shot measurement error as an approximation error and suppresses it by taking more measurements. This is the point that our work seeks to handle differently. Reducing the measurement and sampling cost of QC is therefore a line of research in its own right. Existing schemes include allocating measurements across different observables in variational algorithms, and constructing classical estimates of a quantum state from a small number of measurements [ 38 , 37 , 9 , 17 , 2 , 11 , 14 ] . What these methods share is the goal of keeping the estimation error small with limited measures. Meanwhile, our starting point is different from both threads above. Generally speaking, the quantum diffusion works assume the requirement of an accurate readout and pay for it. The measurement-frugal works minimize the estimation error under a shot budget. Both therefore treat the error as something to be made small. Instead of minimizing the readout error, we only seek to limit it such that the generation procedure can work normally, making a covariance matching problem instead of minimizing. Where such condition holds, the sampler reduces the injected-noise covariance by the covariance already contributed by measurement. The shot count is then an output of the condition rather than a hyperparameter to be tuned, and it is what our adaptive schedule implements. I-C Contributions The contribution of this work mainly lies on a QC mechanism for diffusion model applications. We turn the finite-shot noise of a quantum readout from a liability into a resource the sampler can spend, and we give the condition that says how far it can be spent. The specific contributions are as follows. • We identify the injected-noise covariance of a stochastic diffusion sampler as a budget for finite-shot readout noise, allowing quantum measurement fluctuations to replace part of the externally generated noise. • We derive a positive-semidefinite (PSD) condition for matching the total conditional noise covariance to that of the shot-noise-free reverse step, and solve it for a state-dependent shot budget. With the true covariance and conditionally independent residual noise, this gives exact covariance matching for the linear update, which additionally relies on the Gaussian approximation to the readout error. • We supply the encoding and the trainable readout that the mechanism needs, placing the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex so that the Born-measurement output is compatible with the denoising task. • We validate the method on a Gaussian mixture and on MNIST in a learned latent space, achieving comparable quality on the reported metrics with far fewer measurements. III-A Hybrid Encoding for Quantum Diffusion Models For a DM, the encoding is not a free design choice, and we begin by making the constraint that fixes it explicit. A DM applies its denoiser iteratively. The output of one reverse step is the input of the next, so the encoding and the readout must live in the same space. On the quantum side the readout is fixed by physics, since measuring in the computational basis returns Born probabilities and the output of the circuit therefore always lies in the simplex 𝒫 N − 1 \mathcal{P}^{N-1} . The input must consequently be placed on the simplex as well, and probability encoding, which loads p i \sqrt{p_{i}} into the amplitude of | i ⟩ \ket{i} , is the encoding that the problem selects. The other two encodings of Section II-B play different roles here. Angle encoding uses one qubit per data dimension, and we adopt it in Section IV-C , where a low data dimension makes it affordable. Amplitude encoding is more expressive per qubit, but its output is a probability vector while its input is a signed amplitude vector, so the two do not live in the same space and the denoiser cannot be iterated without an extra and costly reconstruction step. Probability encoding leaves one resource untouched. It fixes only the moduli of the amplitudes and says nothing about their phases, so the azimuthal degrees of freedom of the state are unused. A DM, in turn, must supply its denoiser with one quantity beyond the noisy sample, namely the current diffusion step, which is conventionally injected through a time embedding. The information the denoiser has to carry is thus exactly the information the encoding has room for.
